newsitem.title: MEXICO: In Mexico's south, politicians campaign the old way.
newsitem.headline: In Mexico's south, politicians campaign the old way.

text.p: The left-wing opposition has cut into the ruling party's power base in this oil-rich southeastern state but the almost feudal politics of provincial Mexico mean their candidate faces an uphill struggle in elections on July 6.

While the government in Mexico City is keen to promote the country as a sturdy democracy, out in states like Campeche the opposition says ruling party bosses use carrot-and-stick tactics to win over peasants with just three years schooling.
But for the first time in its 68-year history, the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) is feeling the heat in Campeche from an opposition candidate.

Layda Sansores San Roman, the scion of a political family with huge clout in the state, quit her post as a PRI senator last year to join the left-wing Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD) and contest the governorship.
Support is growing. Prawn fishermen whose livelihood has been hurt by pollution from the local oil industry have painted their fishing boats yellow, the colour of the PRD.
A survey in the national El Universal newspaper last week gave PRI candidate for Campeche governor Antonio Gonzalez Curi 31.8 percent of the vote against 25.6 percent for Sansores.

But 36.3 percent did not reply. Pollsters say this is often because respondents fear reprisals if they express support for the opposition. If only a third of the no-replies were PRD voters, then the opposition could beat the PRI.
"This is a vital election," the PRI's Gonzalez Curi told a breakfast for Ciudad del Carmen's business leaders, referring to the state's huge oil reserves. "The President has his eyes on Campeche."
Sansores knows what she is up against.
"Campeche is very primitive in its democratic development," she said in an interview aboard her campaign bus. "Here there are tricks, repression and threats."

On election day her team will be watching for Mexico's traditional vote-rigging tactics -- "pregnant ballot boxes" pre-stuffed with ballot papers favouring the ruling party, or "tacos" -- fistfuls of extra ballots folded together as one.

Just weeks ago the PRD says two carpenters filed a complaint after finding stacks of voting papers stashed in an apartment belonging to a PRI supporter. Official investigators arrived five days later and found the apartment empty.
Sansores also claims the PRI is using traditional vote-buying techniques, such as throwing lunches for villages of hungry peasants or promising cash to fix their houses.
Nor is the press immune from pressure. Photographers trailing Sansores from unmarked vehicles equipped with radio antennae take pictures of reporters covering her campaign.

Last month the newspaper Reforma alleged that PRI activists in Campeche had diverted medicines from state health clinics, re-labelled them with the PRI logo and candidate's name, and handed them out to voters. The PRI denied any wrongdoing, saying the medicines were legally acquired.

"If people criticise us for giving free medicines, bought in pharmacies for poor peasants, let them criticise us," Gonzalez Curi, dangling his two-year-old son on the rostrum, told a meeting of housing estate leaders.
"We have always given medicines and we always will -- people from outside Campeche don't know how we work."
Local resident Rosamarie Perez Santiago, 33, surveyed a line of buses used to ferry in supporters from nearby suburbs to a Gonzalez Curi rally later in the day.
"The PRI give us medicines, donations, and offer us free drinks and T-shirts," she says. "But it's the same as always -- promises promises, and nothing ever changes."
The PRD also claims that Gonzalez Curi has spent seven times more than his 4.86 million peso ($615,000) legal limit.
Gonzalez Curi denies the allegation. "Does this look like an ostentatious campaign to you?" he asks after a lunch of tacos and soft drinks with the taxi drivers' union.
"It's a very austere campaign based on the structure the PRI has in every state...We have spent up until today approximately three million pesos ($380,000)."
